newsitem.title: USA: Boycott set on biotech US corn, soybeans - Activists.
newsitem.headline: Boycott set on biotech US corn, soybeans - Activists.

text.p: A coalition of small U.S. consumer and environmental groups announced Monday a global boycott of genetically altered corn and soybeans and targeted 10 foods from Coca-Cola Co to McDonald's Corp french fries.

Long-time biotechnology foe Jeremy Rifkin announced the boycott at a news conference that included appeals from a European trade group for labeling of bio-foods so that consumers could decide whether to buy them.
Both crops have U.S. approval for marketing.

The European Union has approved sale of the gene-altered soybeans and has yet to decide on the corn. The soybean was adapted for tolerance to a weed-killer. The corn produces a naturally occuring pesticide to repel the damaging corn borer.
Rifkin said 300 groups in 48 nations would take part in the boycott. Leaders of the 10 targeted U.S. foods were being asked to pledge not to use the biotech crops.
"We have not had response yet. It is still early," he said, saying it was still the "early hours of a campaign that could last for years."

Heinrich Kroener, secretary general of EuroCommerce, said labels on bio-foods would calm consumer food concerns. He pointed to this year's "mad cow" crisis and earlier scandals over improper drug use to fatten European livestock.

"I can't ask for a boycott, a total boycott," Kroener said, but warned that several major members of his group would not accept U.S. soybeans without assurance they were not the genetically altered variety.
Bill Christison of the National Family Farm Coalition, said labeling was impractical. "The numerous problems could easily be solved if the gene splicers would just go away."

U.S. officials say both products are safe and there was no reason to block them from sale or to require special labels because they are indistinguishable from other varieties. Like industry groups, U.S. officials say labeling is impractical considering the huge volume of U.S. corn and oilseeds.
Two U.S. trade groups, Grocery Manufacturers of America and Natioal Food Processors Association, supported the safety of biotech foods.
"Consumers should instead be warned of Mr Rifkin continuing to spread his weed-like misinformation," the GMA said.
